title: Mputa Stew
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Deep-fried Nile perch simmered in a thick groundnut sauce with eggplant, carrot and green pepper — the stew Ugandans make when the fish is good enough to deserve it.
longDesc: Nile perch is mputa, and it runs from a palm's length to enormous. It is fleshy and aromatic enough that Ugandans have a stew built specifically around it: thick groundnut paste, the fish already deep-fried so it holds together, and vegetables that go in almost raw and wilt in the sauce. The groundnut paste must be loosened with water and mashed to a thick but runny paste before it goes in, which is the same rule that governs every groundnut sauce in the country.
ingredients: A handful of green onions, to garnish
equipment: Bowl and wooden spoon, for the groundnut paste
steps: Put a saucepan over high heat, add the oil and the garlic, and let the garlic brown a little.
Add the onions, tomatoes and salt, then add the fish pieces.
Add the green pepper, the eggplants, the carrots and the chilli oil if using.
Stir until the vegetables wilt a little.
In a bowl, put the groundnut paste with a little water and mash it with a wooden spoon until you have a thick but runny paste.
Pour the paste into the saucepan with the fish and stir well.
Add 2 to 3 cups of water and bring the stew to the boil.
Once it has boiled, add the black pepper, stir, and let it simmer 20 to 30 minutes.
Take it off the heat, garnish with chopped green onions and serve.
chefTips: Fry the fish before it goes into the stew. Raw perch falls apart in a groundnut sauce and you lose the pieces.
Mash the groundnut paste with water first, to thick-but-runny. Spooned in neat it sits in lumps and never disperses.
Half a teaspoon of oil is all the recipe uses — the groundnuts carry the fat.
The vegetables only wilt at that stage. They finish in the simmer.
Twenty to thirty minutes of simmering is what marries the groundnut and the fish. Rushed, it tastes like two things in a pan.
Tilapia works if perch is not available, and it is what many Ugandan households actually use.
This is the quantified version of a dish the author showed on television and then never published on her blog — it only ever appeared in her ebook.
commonMistakes: Cooking the vegetables down before the sauce goes in.
Adding all the water at once before the paste is in.
sources: Adapted from Sophia Musoki's Mputa (Nile Perch) Stew, printed in her free ebook 16 Ugandan Dishes to Make — all quantities and the method are hers. Her blog post on the dish (February 2016, tied to a CNN African Voices appearance) said only 'RECIPE COMING SOON' and the recipe never appeared there.

The market context — that Nile perch is mputa, that the size varies from a palm's length to larger than life, and that the stew is one Ugandans pride themselves on making — is from that blog headnote.
reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water. Groundnut sauces thicken as they sit.
healthBenefits: Nile perch is high in protein, omega-3 and vitamin D.
Groundnuts add plant protein, niacin, folate and vitamin E.
Eggplant, carrot, tomato and pepper make it a complete plate on its own.
culturalNote: Nile perch was introduced into Lake Victoria in the mid twentieth century and remade the lake's ecology and its economy at the same time — it is both a major export and a genuine environmental story. The stew is what happens domestically with a fish that is mostly filleted for Europe.
